questions.prompt: What two properties must a problem have to be solvable by dynamic programming?

options.text: The greedy-choice property and a sorted input
A balanced tree and no cycles

questions.explanation: The same subproblems must recur (so caching pays off) and an optimal solution must be built from optimal solutions of subproblems. Without overlap, plain divide-and-conquer suffices.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between memoisation and tabulation?

options.text: Memoisation is top-down and lazy; tabulation is bottom-up and iterative
Tabulation uses recursion; memoisation uses loops

questions.explanation: Memoisation recurses and caches results as they are first needed, so it computes only reachable states. Tabulation fills a table iteratively from the base cases upward, avoiding recursion overhead.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of the standard 0/1 knapsack dynamic program for n items and capacity W?
questions.explanation: The table has n rows and W columns, each filled in constant time. This is pseudo-polynomial: W is a value, not an input length, so it is exponential in the number of bits of W.

questions.prompt: Memoising the naive recursive Fibonacci reduces its time complexity from exponential to:
questions.explanation: There are only n distinct subproblems, each computed once and reused thereafter. The exponential blow-up came entirely from recomputing the same values.

questions.prompt: The longest increasing subsequence of an array can be found in O(n log n) using:

options.text: A greedy scan without any auxiliary structure
Patience sorting with binary search over the tails array

questions.explanation: Maintaining an array of smallest possible tail values and binary-searching each element's insertion point gives O(n log n). The straightforward DP is O(n^2).

questions.prompt: The unbounded coin-change problem (minimum coins to make an amount, unlimited coins) has a DP time complexity of:

options.text: O(amount x number of coin types)

questions.explanation: For each amount from 1 to the target, the DP tries every coin denomination, giving amount x coins work. It is again pseudo-polynomial in the amount.

questions.prompt: When is a greedy algorithm preferable to dynamic programming for a problem both can solve?

options.text: Only when the input is unsorted
When the greedy-choice property holds, since greedy is typically faster and simpler

questions.explanation: If a locally optimal choice is provably part of a global optimum, greedy avoids building a table and runs faster. DP is the safe fallback when that property cannot be established.

questions.prompt: In many 1-D dynamic programs such as climbing stairs, the space can be reduced from O(n) to O(1) because:

options.text: The recursion has no base case
Each state depends only on a constant number of previous states
The problem has no overlapping subproblems

questions.explanation: When dp[i] uses only dp[i-1] and dp[i-2], keeping those two values in variables suffices and the full table is unnecessary. This rolling-variable trick is a common optimisation.

questions.prompt: The subset-sum problem (does a subset sum to a target T?) has a DP complexity of:
questions.explanation: A boolean table over items and achievable sums up to T is filled in O(nT). Like knapsack it is pseudo-polynomial, and the decision version is the basis for the NP-complete partition problem.

questions.prompt: Why is the 0/1 knapsack DP called pseudo-polynomial rather than polynomial?

options.text: It only works for small n
It uses recursion instead of iteration
Its running time is polynomial in the numeric value W, which is exponential in W's bit length

questions.explanation: The input size of W is its number of bits, roughly log W, so O(nW) is exponential in that size. A truly polynomial algorithm would be polynomial in the bit length of the input.
